title: Files and Select-String
summary: Walk folder trees with the flags that matter, search logs with Select-String (grep that returns objects), and handle file names with square brackets.

steps.title: Walking the file system
body: ```powershell
Get-ChildItem C:\Logs -Recurse -File -Filter *.log     # every .log file below C:\Logs
Get-ChildItem . -Recurse -Depth 1 -Directory            # folders, at most one level down
Get-ChildItem ~ -Force                                  # include hidden files (dot files on Linux)
Test-Path C:\Logs\app.log                               # True / False; -PathType Leaf or Container
Join-Path $PSScriptRoot 'config' 'app.json'             # builds a path with the right separator
Split-Path C:\Logs\web\access.log -Leaf                 # access.log  (-Parent gives C:\Logs\web)
New-Item C:\Reports\2026 -ItemType Directory -Force     # creates it and its parents; no error if it exists
**`-Filter` versus `-Include`:** `-Filter *.log` is passed to the file system itself, so only matching names come
back: fast on a network share with a million files. `-Include` and `-Exclude` are applied by PowerShell after
reading everything, and they accept several patterns (`-Include *.log, *.txt`). Use `-Filter` when one pattern is
enough.
`Copy-Item`, `Move-Item` and `Remove-Item` take objects from the pipeline, and **all of them support `-WhatIf`**:
`... | Remove-Item -WhatIf` prints what *would* be deleted and deletes nothing. Run it first, every time.

steps.prompt: On Linux, what does this print?
steps.explain: Since PowerShell 6, `Join-Path` takes any number of child parts. On Windows the same lines would use `\`. Build paths with `Join-Path` rather than string concatenation and you never get `C:\Logs\\app.log` or a missing separator.

steps.title: Select-String: grep that returns objects
body: `Select-String` searches text with a regular expression, like `grep`, but each hit is a **`MatchInfo` object**:
```powershell
Select-String -Path ~/logs/*.log -Pattern 'timed out'
billing.log:57:2026-11-26T09:00:56Z ERROR upstream timed out after 30 s (req bi-4056)
That line is only how it is *displayed*. The object has `Filename`, `Path`, `LineNumber`, `Line` and `Matches`
(the regex matches, with their groups), so you can keep working with it:
```powershell
Select-String -Path ~/logs/*.log -Pattern 'timed out' | Group-Object Filename -NoElement
Select-String -Path ~/logs/*.log -Pattern 'req (\w+-\d+)' | ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value }
| Switch | Does |
| `-SimpleMatch` | the pattern is plain text, not a regex (for `$`, `(`, `.` in what you search) |
| `-CaseSensitive` | match case (the default ignores it, unlike grep) |
| `-Context 2, 3` | also keep 2 lines before and 3 after each hit |
| `-NotMatch` | lines that do **not** match |
| `-List` | only the first hit per file ("which files mention it?") |
| `-Raw` | PowerShell 7: output just the matching lines as strings |

steps.title: Where did the timeouts happen?
prompt: The on-call engineer wants every **upstream timeout** (lines containing `timed out`) across the service logs
`~/logs/*.log`, as a CSV they can open: `~/answers/timeouts.csv` with exactly the columns **`Filename`** and

checks.name: timeouts.csv lists every timeout
cmd: if not os.path.exists(p): sys.exit('~/answers/timeouts.csv does not exist yet')
if cols != ['Filename', 'LineNumber']: sys.exit(f'columns are {cols[:5]}, expected Filename, LineNumber')
out = subprocess.run('cd ~/logs && grep -n "timed out" *.log', shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
want = sorted((l.split(':')[0], l.split(':')[1]) for l in out.splitlines())
got = sorted((r['Filename'], r['LineNumber']) for r in rows)
if got != want: sys.exit(f'{len(got)} rows, expected {len(want)}; first expected: {want[:3]}')
checks.fail: Not quite: see what the check found.

hints: `Select-String -Path ~/logs/*.log -Pattern 'timed out'` finds them. Pipe one hit to `Get-Member` to see its properties.
`Filename` and `LineNumber` are properties of each hit, so `Select-Object Filename, LineNumber` keeps just those.
solution: Select-String -Path ~/logs/*.log -Pattern 'timed out' | Select-Object Filename, LineNumber | Export-Csv -Path ~/answers/timeouts.csv
steps.explain: On Windows, `Select-String` is the answer to "there is no grep": it reads any text file, handles encodings, and its objects export straight to CSV. For huge trees, `rg` (ripgrep) is faster still; `Select-String` wins when you want objects back.

steps.title: Square brackets are wildcards
body: In `-Path`, PowerShell expands **wildcards**: `*`, `?` and **`[abc]`** (one of these characters). So
`report[2026-10].txt` does not mean that file; it means `report` + *one character from 2, 0, 2, 6-1, 0* + `.txt`.
Nothing matches, and many cmdlets then do **nothing at all, without an error**.
Every file cmdlet has a **`-LiteralPath`** parameter that takes the name exactly as written:
```powershell
Get-Item -LiteralPath 'report[2026-10].txt'
Move-Item -LiteralPath $file -Destination ~/archive
Use single quotes so `$` and backticks stay literal too. Objects piped from `Get-ChildItem` are bound by their
`LiteralPath`, so `Get-ChildItem ~/inbox -Filter 'report*' | Move-Item -Destination ~/archive` is safe. In scripts that
receive paths from users or other systems, prefer `-LiteralPath`.

steps.title: Archive the reports with brackets in their names
prompt: A reporting tool drops files like `report[2026-10].txt` into `~/inbox`. Try the obvious first:
Move **both** `report[...]` files into `~/archive`. Leave `summary[final].txt` and `notes.txt` in the inbox.

checks.name: and gone from the inbox
checks.fail: The reports should be moved, not copied.

checks.name: the other files stay
checks.fail: `summary[final].txt` and `notes.txt` should still be in `~/inbox`, and only the two reports in `~/archive`.

hints: The first `Move-Item` did nothing: `[2026-10]` was read as a wildcard character class.
`Move-Item -LiteralPath '~/inbox/report[2026-10].txt' -Destination ~/archive` takes the name as written (`~` still works). Or let `Get-ChildItem` find both.
steps.explain: The same trap bites `Remove-Item`: a clean-up that silently skips every file with `[` in its name. When a file cmdlet "does nothing", check the name for `[`, `]`, `*` or `?`, and switch to `-LiteralPath` or to piping the objects.

steps.prompt: Put a safe clean-up of old exports in order.
steps.explain: Collect the list once, look at how much it is, rehearse with `-WhatIf`, then delete exactly the same list. Re-running `Get-ChildItem` between the rehearsal and the real run could delete something else.

steps.prompt: You need every `.log` and `.txt` file under `\\fs01\share`, which holds two million files. Which line is right and fast?
steps.explain: `-Filter` takes one pattern and is applied by the file system, so each run only transfers matching names over the network. `-Include` and `Where-Object` are correct but read all two million entries first. `-Filter` does not accept a list.
